rounds.text: Propshop Events and Exhibitions Ltd is exceptionally under-appreciated by the market, trading at a modest P/E of 12.9x [E1] despite exhibiting phenomenal operational profitability and capital efficiency. The company boasts a stellar ROCE of 57.03% and ROE of 41.46% (per data provider key-ratios), which completely dwarf the broader sector benchmarks of 6.61% and 5.08% respectively [E5, E6, E7]. This elite return profile is underpinned by robust growth, highlighted by a 3-year compounded sales growth of 40% and a blistering 102% compounded profit growth over the same period [E10, E12]. Furthermore, the valuation implies an unjustifiably pessimistic outlook, with a reverse DCF indicating that the current market price only prices in a meager 2.0% earnings growth against an 18.0% base-case assumption [E30]. The business is virtually debt-free with a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.01x [E21], and intrinsic value models suggest a massive 68.5% margin of safety [E28, E29]. Conceded: debtor days have increased from 40.2 to 56.8 days [E36], and cash conversion for Mar 2025 stands at a low 0.02x [E20].

Despite high headline profitability metrics, Propshop Events and Exhibitions Ltd exhibits severe cash flow disconnection, with a cash conversion ratio of just 0.02x operating cash flow against reported profit for Mar 2025, which signals that profits are far ahead of cash and points to underlying issues with receivables or accruals [E20]. This warning is reinforced by the company's debtor days, which have worsened significantly by increasing from 40.2 to 56.8 days [E36]. Furthermore, operating margins are inconsistent over both the last two years and the last two quarters [E18, E19], and the company trades at a price-to-book ratio of 2.53x, which is elevated compared to the sector benchmark of 1.42x [E5]. Although the company is largely debt-free, its borrowings ticked up to Rs 0.17 Cr in Mar 2026 from Rs 0.00 Cr a year earlier [E22], and the stock provides no dividend yield at 0.00% [E3]. Conceded: the company boasts a high three-year compounded profit growth of 102% and an impressive three-year median return on equity of 64% [E12, E15].

Conceded: cash conversion read 0.02x for Mar 2025 [E20], and debtor days increased from 40.2 to 56.8 [E36]. However, these temporary working capital frictions do not overshadow the extraordinary operational velocity of the business, evidenced by a 3-year compounded sales growth of 40% [E10] and a 3-year compounded profit growth of 102% [E12]. The bear's concern over inconsistent operating margins [E18, E19] ignores the structural margin expansion that has lifted the operating margin to 16% in Mar 2026, a six percentage point improvement over three years [E17]. While the price-to-book ratio is 2.53x against a sector benchmark of 1.42x [E5], this premium is entirely justified by elite capital efficiency, featuring an ROE of 41.46% and an ROCE of 57.03% compared to sector benchmarks of 5.08% and 6.61% respectively [E6, E7]. The nominal increase in borrowings to Rs 0.17 Cr is negligible [E22], leaving the company virtually debt-free with a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.01x [E21], while the lack of a dividend yield [E3] simply reflects aggressive reinvestment powering rapid growth. Finally, the market grossly under-appreciates this profile, pricing the stock at a modest P/E of 12.9 [E1] despite a reverse DCF showing today's price implies a mere 2.0% earnings growth against a base-case expectation of 18.0% [E30].

Conceded: 3-year compounded sales growth is 40% [E10] and profit growth is 102% [E12]. However, the bull minimizes profound cash generation alarms by dismissing cash conversion of just 0.02x for Mar 2025 where profits far outpaced actual cash, pointing directly to severe receivables and accrual distortions [E20]. This collection friction is confirmed by debtor days deteriorating from 40.2 to 56.8 days [E36], revealing that explosive top-line gains are heavily reliant on uncollected paper profits rather than real liquidity. The bull's dismissal of margin trends is contradicted by official records noting that both yearly and quarterly operating-margin trends are inconsistent over the recent periods [E18, E19]. Furthermore, while the P/B premium is defended through stellar returns, the company pays a dividend yield of 0.00% [E3], meaning shareholders bear all the risk of locked-up working capital without any direct cash return. Finally, the nominal borrowing increase to Rs 0.17 Cr [E22] breaks a clean zero-debt record, and trading at 2.53x P/B against a 1.42x sector benchmark [E5] exposes investors to a multiple derating if cash collections fail to materialize.
